forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton told in October it will receive £12.7m towards a £14.1m SEND deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Wolverhampton City Council was formally notified in October 2026 that it will receive a High Needs Stability Grant of £12.7m, 90% of an accrued deficit of £14.1m on special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) at 31 March 2026. The council's 2027-2028 draft revenue budget and medium term plan, put to the Health Scrutiny Panel, says this leaves £1.4m "to fund initially".

The deficit sits in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The paper says the grant is available subject to a local SEND reform plan. It also says a £2.0m provision is made in 2028-2029 for any remaining deficit, and that the options for funding beyond that are unclear.

The council's general fund risk register, an appendix to the same papers, lists the end of the SEND statutory accounting override among its government policy risks. The override is a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet. The register names it alongside NHS restructuring, the Social Care Fair Pay Policy and the UK Emissions Trading Scheme, and rates the government policy risk Red.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton Council asks to raise its capitalisation budget from £2m to £4.561m for transformation projects
news_drafts.lead:
Wolverhampton Council is asking its full Council meeting on 2 December to approve an increase in its "Capitalisation Directives" budget line from £2m to £4.561m, a rise of £2.561m.

The detailed forecast appendix to the report attributes the increase to "additional use of capital receipts flexibility to fund specific transformational projects". Capital receipts flexibility is the rule that lets a council use money from selling assets on the costs of changing how services are run. The report says: "Approval for the increase is sought in this report."

The papers set out the approved figure, the proposed figure and the change. They do not name the transformation projects in this appendix.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton notified of £12.7m grant against £14.1m high needs deficit, leaving £1.4m to fund
news_drafts.lead:
Wolverhampton council was formally notified in October 2026 that it will receive £12.7m, 90%, in High Needs Stability Grant funding. The council's accrued high needs deficit stood at £14.1m at 31 March 2026. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The notification leaves the council, in its own words, "with £1.4 million to fund initially".

The figures are in the draft 2027-2028 revenue budget and medium term financial strategy, which goes to the Economy and Growth Scrutiny Panel on 25 November. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, runs until March 2028. The council's 2028-2029 forecast includes £2.0m to cover any remaining deficit.

The general fund risk register, an appendix to the same papers, rates the risk from changes to government policy as Red. It lists NHS restructuring, the Social Care Fair Pay Policy, the UK Emissions Trading Scheme and the end of the SEND statutory accounting override among the risks that might materialise.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2027-2028 Draft Revenue Budget and Medium Term
findings.headline: No new savings required for 2027-2028 beyond increased Productivity and Efficiency targets; new savings likely needed from 2028-2029
findings.detail: The paper says the increase to Productivity and Efficiency targets is the only new saving projected for 2027-2028. From 2028-2029 new savings are expected to be needed to close the remaining gap.
findings.matters: A council signalling that new savings will be needed from a named year gives a finance director and lender a specific date to test the plan against.
findings.quote: it is likely that new savings will need to be identified for 2028-2029 onwards

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2027-2028 Draft Revenue Budget and Medium Term
findings.headline: External auditor reported no significant weaknesses in 2024-2025 Value for Money arrangements
findings.detail: The paper says early indications are that the 2025-2026 report will reach the same conclusion. The auditor's assessment covers financial sustainability, governance and economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.matters: A value-for-money conclusion without significant weaknesses is the external auditor's view a lender and peer will check first.
findings.quote: They formally reported on our Value for Money arrangements through the Annual Auditors Report for 2024-2025 that they had found no significant weaknesses in the Council’s arrangements

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2027-2028 Draft Revenue Budget and Medium Term
findings.headline: Savings proposal on district parking fees and charges removed from the OFC savings target
findings.detail: The paper says parking will remain free in Tettenhall, Bilston and for three hours in Wednesfield, and that a city-wide review of parking is underway.
findings.matters: A savings target removed rather than delivered changes the savings base a council has to rely on, which lenders and peers should see.
findings.quote: the savings proposal in relation to district parking fees and charges has been removed.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2027-2028 Draft Revenue Budget and Medium Term
findings.headline: Fees and charges amendments projected to add £551,000 of income in 2027-2028, with a further £208,000 in 2028-2029
findings.detail: The changes were approved through Individual Executive Decision Notices, mostly from October 2026. The paper says the 2028-2029 figure could be subject to change.
findings.matters: Income from fees and charges is a lever many councils are using, and the amount and timing of the uplift is a comparable number.
findings.quote: This has resulted in projected additional income of £551,000 across a number of council services in 2027-2028.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2027-2028 Draft Revenue Budget and Medium Term
findings.headline: Households in temporary accommodation down 18.2% under the Housing Advice and Temporary Accommodation project
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction allows the temporary accommodation contingency to be reduced, while demand remains a risk. The number owed the main homelessness duty fell to a two-year low.
findings.matters: A demand reduction linked to a specific project, and the contingency released against it, is a concrete example of a demand pressure being reversed.
findings.figures: 18.2% reduction in households in temporary accommodation; 21% reduction in households owed the main homelessness duty
findings.quote: This has resulted in an 18.2% reduction in the number of households in temporary accommodation and a 21% reduction in the number owed the main homelessness duty

daily_post.headline: £770,000 of capital and £3.0 million of revenue investment is refocused on council priorities, including £1.0 million from short-term grants.
daily_post.lead: Using an underspend and forecast headroom to fund capital and recurrent investment is a choice other councils are making, and the recurrent share is a commitment that will persist.
